articles.title: Best Driving Skills to Practice Before Your Teen Drives Alone
articles.h1: Best Driving Skills to Practice Before Your Teen Drives Alone
articles.meta: Learn the essential driving skills to practice before your teen drives alone, from hazard scanning and speed choice to night driving and practice logs.
articles.excerpt: Teen driving skills are best built through supervised practice that reflects real road conditions. Before your teen drives alone, the hours you spend beside them should go toward hazard scanning, choosing a safe speed, managing distractions, and recognizing when a situation is beyond what they can handle yet. Parking-lot control and smooth steering are a fine place to start, and a busy street is where your new driver learns the habits that get them home safely. Research suggests that vehicle handling is rarely the deciding factor when a novice driver gets into trouble. In an undated analysis citing Edwards (2001), the California Department of Motor Vehicles reported that poor vehicle control accounts for only 10% of novice driver crashes in the United States, with the remaining ninety percent stemming from inexperience, inaccurate risk perception, overconfidence, and risky choices. Key takeaways Novice driver crash risk stems primarily from deficits in hazard scanning, speed management, and distraction rather than basic vehicle handling. Legal practice hour requirements represent a statutory floor, whereas real driving competence often requires between 65 and 120 hours of supervised driving. Commentary driving turns passive observation into an active habit by having teens verbally identify developing hazards. Practicing after dark and in adverse weather is critical, as over half of fatal teen crashes occur during nighttime hours. Distraction routines, including setting playlists and navigation before shifting into gear, should be established during early practice. Evaluating readiness through an observational checklist helps identify specific maneuvers that require additional supervised practice. Driving skills to practice before solo driving A complete list of driving skills to practice covers mechanical handling, roadway rules, and real-time risk assessment. Novice drivers must master mechanical controls first, but higher-order visual search and attention habits carry far more weight once an adult is no longer sitting in the passenger seat. Research from the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia identified three primary skill deficits that account for nearly half of serious teen crashes: scanning and reacting to hazards, managing speed across different environments, and managing distraction.
